So these were my tasks, and sometime toward the end of April, we issued several bulletins on ordinary paper, A4, daily, about 100 copies per day and we distributed it among the population so that they could know at least some basic things about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me what did you do in May, 1992, in your field of activity? But first, what was the situation with the Serbs in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, those were critical days for the civilian authorities in Samac, since a major -- major pressure was being brought by the families from Odzak, that is, those who had found refuge in the municipality of Samac and then relatives, relations of Serbs incarcerated in Odzak. They were coming from Germany, Austria, Switzerland, where they were migrant workers and they were bringing pressure on the authorities in the municipality of Samac to help those people. Concretely, my father was in prison. My mother was in isolation. And I was very worried about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me concretely what was done? What steps did the Crisis Staff take in May to solve the problem?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Crisis Staff sent a series of letters to various addressees with a view to helping, even though I don't think that those letters served much purpose, because the Crisis Staff did not really -- wasn't really vested with any serious power, with any proper authority, to resolve the problem. I know that, for instance, a letter was sent to the federal executive council. I mean the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, and perhaps to some other addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And were you personally involved in some activities relative to the attempts to get Serbs incarcerated in Odzak released?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Describe it to us.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was more or less like this: We did not know exactly how many people were incarcerated there. So we are talking about Serbs from localities of Novi Grad, Nova Dubica, Trnjak and some others from Odzak and from other villages too. Since in order to get some basic information and try to intercede through the Red Cross to come by some more precise information, the Crisis Staff designated Mr. Miroslav Tadic, Simo Zaric and me to try to put together lists of those people, and since we come from those places, that is, Mr. Tadic is from Novi Grad, I'm from Dubica and Mr. Tadic [As interpreted] is from Trnjak, I, for instance, compiled this list on the basis of records and with the help of the -- of the family members of those Serbs who came from Dubica --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Says Mr. Tadic is from Trnjak. On line 18, page 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It should read Mr. Zaric, that's what he said, and it's obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the correction, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat this?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This work group that was of a temporary nature, consisted of Mr. Tadic, Miroslav Tadic, who is from Novi Grad. Myself, and Mr. Zaric, who is from Trnjak, and I am from Donja Dubica. The task of this group was to try to compile a list of persons who were in prison, detention, isolation, in Odzak. Specifically, I was the one who compiled this list for Donja Dubica, primarily with the assistance of members of families that were in Samac, and their families were in Odzak. When these lists were compiled, as far as I know, Mr. Tadic handed them over to the Red Cross, and in this way, the purpose for this working group had ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any contacts with the other side, with the Odzak side, the Croats?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any contacts, but I think that Mr. Tadic and Mr. Zaric had contact through radio links. That was the only means of communication. And this was at the centre for reporting and monitoring. There were some contacts. And in part, I attended one of these contacts. When I entered the centre where the radio transmitters were, that is where Kosta Simic was. Kosta Simic was one of the employees who worked there. I knew him he was a colleague from work. Mr. Simo Zaric was on the radio with some person from Odzak and there was yet another person whom I did not know. There was a fierce verbal duel going on. The person on the other side, from Odzak, was making a lot of noise, swearing and saying, when the HVO would come and take Samac, that they would hang Simo Zaric. I'll be vulgar, but I'll say what this person said, "Hang him by the balls."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what do you know about the final resolution of the problem of the Serbs in Odzak in the course of May or June? What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the International Red Cross that made efforts in that area. Then there was an exchange at the Bosna River, near Zasavica in the month of May. I think it was the end of May. I cannot say what the exact date was. The other exchange was in Lipovac. That is on the border between Croatia and Serbia. This was on the 4th of July. This was when my father got out of prison. So my father was exchanged in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, when was this operation finally over, if I can put it that way, this exchange or rather the pulling out of the Serbs from Odzak? It was in July, you put it that way. That's when it was all over, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, later, I was engaged in my own line of work as head of the department and I did not devote enough attention to that particular matter, but I think that there were authorities that had contacts with regard to those particular matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is your personal knowledge regarding the following? Where were Serbs who came from Odzak in that period temporarily accommodated?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serb houses for the most part, in Samac, Kruskovo Polje, Pisari, Skaric and so on. Specifically, I lived at my sister's in Skaric and that's where my mother and my father also came.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have some inconsistencies here in the transcript. Line 17 and 19 on page 92, it looks like two answers and I believe that Mr. Pantelic should look at it and try to clarify it. It seems that something is confused here. Maybe line 17, 18 and 19. So I believe that line 17 should go under the question posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that. There is an inconsistency with the questions and answers in the transcript. I will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you the following: To the best of your knowledge -- now this is my question. When did this process end, of pulling the Serbs out of Odzak, if I can put it that way? When were they coming to the territory of Samac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the overall process?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it took about two or three years, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Next question: You gave that answer regarding the accommodation, where they were staying. Do you know about the Crisis Staff and the executive council, what their activities were in relation to resolving the problem of putting these people up at the villages that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, with regard to these particular matters, the Crisis Staff did have some sessions. The refugees had to be taken care of. This is a very sensitive humanitarian issue. Work was done in this regard, and I think there was a document dedicated to this, which asks for taking refugees in Serb areas for conducting the necessary preparations for taking care of them properly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the rationalisation of space in Serb villages. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say that, I mean that if there was a household, if there was one house, then that house should take in one or two persons into one room and then this -- these people would have access to the bathroom, to the kitchen, et cetera. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me now, this activity in the Crisis Staff, first of all, the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, we know that clashes broke out in Samac. Tell me, where were you on the 17th of April, 1992? And could you explain this to us a bit? What did you do, what for, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th, I went to Belgrade on official business, and I came back in the evening, say around 8.00 in the evening. I came to the secretariat. There was a person at the communications centre who was on duty, and they were on the same floor where the secretariat was. Then Ilija Lukic was there, who was on duty. I found out from him that the bridge could not be crossed, the bridge on the Bosna River. That is to say, that there was no traffic, that all traffic had been stopped. On the side of Prud, there was a problem. That's where the problem was. So I could not go home to Dubica, to Donja Dubica. I went to my sister's at Skarici, this is a settlement five kilometres away from Samac. From there, I telephoned my parents, I explained to them what was going on. They were very concerned. They had some information that on the other side of the Sava River in the region of Jarug, that is to say, a Croat village in the Republic of Croatia, that is to say, on the left bank of the Sava River, they had information that members of the National Guards Corps were coming across. Of course, I was afraid for my parents because I could not see them any more. We only had the telephone to communicate, and the situation was getting increasingly complicated. That night, I was at my sister's. In the morning, when I was awakened, my -- by my sister's mother-in-law, if I can put it that way, she's the person who woke me up, explosions were heard, then gunfire. So there was a skirmish, there was fighting, and the sound was coming from the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is your role when you were in the Secretariat for National Defence, when there are such extraordinary circumstances? Where are you supposed to be? Where is your wartime assignment? Where is your post?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was a clerk in charge of civilian defence matters. Milos Bogdanovic was head of this particular authority. He lives in Skarici, by the way, that is to say, the same place where my sister's house is. And my obligation was to report when the situation is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to see my superior, I went there by car. I went to his house. I did not find him on the 17th. It is only in the evening that we managed to see each other. He told me what happened in Samac, namely, that there was a clash in which the paramilitary formations, together with the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia tried to enter town to take town, and that the Yugoslav People's Army, with the assistance of members of the MUP who were ethnic Serbs, that they thwarted this aggressive activity of the formations that I mentioned. So the JNA had under its control the key positions in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you go to town?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you go to town?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening, when he told me about what was going on, he told me that Ilija Lukic got killed, the person I talked to when I came back from Belgrade, when I came to the Secretariat. He told me that that man got killed that night, and that his family should be helped, that they should get help in terms of burying the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was his job? What was Ilija Lukic's job?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Lukic was an employee at the centre for reporting and monitoring. The name of his particular position is operations officer, so they changed every eight hours. They had eight hour shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did you find out? How was this man killed?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I later on found out that his daughter in the early morning hours, I don't know exactly when, in the morning, she phoned him and was afraid because she heard shooting near her own house. He started going home on foot. He could not hear very well. He was a bit hard of hearing. So on his way home, he was killed. He was killed by a bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was your colleague buried?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 18th, we made an effort. I and the late Milos Bogdanovic, who also got killed later, we made efforts in this respect, and he was transported on the 18th in the afternoon to Milosvac and I think he was buried on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during this first period of time, could you please describe your activities during those first few weeks starting mid-April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 18th, I went to town. By then, it was already possible to enter town, although there were many armed men and it was not quite safe to walk around town, wasn't safe yet. Weapons were being taken from persons who possessed them illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How was this activity going on?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I encountered a vehicle, a car, in town, and it had a loud speaker calling upon citizens to hand in weapons that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And on whose behalf was this activity carried out?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when did you join the organisation of civilian life organising the situation? Because after all, it was an emergency, wasn't it? What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After helping the family of Ilija Lukic organise his funeral, I was told that I should report to Mr. Simeon Simic. Mr. Simeon Simic and Milos Bogdanovic agreed that I would be useful on these information assignments, because it was assessed in those circles that I would be useful in such a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, during these first few weeks, was the population informed to the effect that they had to wear white arm bands?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me further --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, perhaps before Mr. Pantelic progresses further, it's just a little bit of confusion, I think, in what the witness has said. Perhaps Mr. Pantelic can assist the Chamber and clarify. The witness said he went to town on the 18th and then he is asked when he joined the organisation of civilian life. And he says that he did that after helping bury Ilija Lukic. Now, he buried Ilija Lukic on the 19th. So I'm just not clear on when he got this assignment to participate in the organisation of civilian life. And it's important for us to know whether it was on the 18th or the 19th, because of other matters. At least there is some confusion in the Prosecution's mind about his position on that and I would be grateful if Mr. Pantelic could clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure the witness has understood your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I don't see that I used this term organisation of civilian life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I had concerns about that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's a matter of translation. My question was related to the civilian institutions. I mean in municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I also had my concern when I read that because it wasn't very clear, so if we could clarify that, if Your Honours please, and secondly, when he got his assignment? Was it the 18th or was it the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have heard my colleague, the Prosecutor. Tell me first, what are these structures at municipal level that were involved in organising or rather resolving the problems faced by the civilian population? Could you mention them?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just repeat this? I think I said this quite clearly. Mr. Milos Bogdanovic, who was officially still my superior, said to me that when he spoke to Simeon Simic, they agreed that I should be engaged in information tasks. I said that. I repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I want to ask you which structures at municipal level were in charge, because there was a state of emergency, the war had started. Who were all the structures involved at municipal level in resolving problems of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a very broad question. In a way, everybody who held a certain post had the duty of establishing contact and trying to organise civilian life. This is the beginning of the war. And that in itself is a state of emergency. And it created commotion. Again, the institutions had to be brought into some kind of order so that they could function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where were meetings held -- where were persons who were engaged in such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution's query, the date when the witness went back to work in these institutions, was it the 18th or the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When were you directly involved in these institutions?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 20th. I said that, the 20th. Not the 18th. It was on the 20th that I started to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where did you start working on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the only place where people belonging to civilian life were gathered, I mean from the civilian authorities, was the agricultural combine, PIK Samac, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps a few days, five, six, seven days. I can't say. That place was not safe because a tank from the Republic of Croatia constantly kept targeting the silo, and that is the tallest building in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Uniglas. That is a company a bit further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For how long was it there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say for 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After that, where was the seat?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the heating plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How often did you attend meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend meetings of the Crisis Staff because I was not a member of the Crisis Staff but there was a telephone and it was at the communications centre too. There was a telephone there as well. So I was there and my job could not be done without having a telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm just trying to follow this evidence and be as clear in my mind as I can. I'm not understanding this and I'm sure the witness could explain to us. He says that he started work on the 20th. He says that he went to Uniglas. He says the heating plant thereafter. What was his job there? What was he doing? Because he hasn't yet explained that. If he had an assignment or a post, then in order for to you understand this evidence, you should know what it was. And it's that that is not clear when I read it, the transcript. So we know where he was but we don't know what he was doing. And that's what I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's an issue for you to explore in cross-examination. There is a problem here in transcript. It's at page 100, line 13. His answer was at Uniglas. And then that's the first part of his answer and the second part is that is a company a bit further away. So this combination answer and question was actually the answer. And now my next question after that was, "For how long was it there?" And then he says 15 days. So there is just for the record, I would like to say that his complete answer was including page -- on page 100 and including line 13 and 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand all that. I've got no problem with that. I've read that. But what was he doing in that period of time? Where he was working can't be any use to you unless you know what he was doing, what his job was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness should answer that. He has heard the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's what I'm -- that's all I'm seeking clarification on. And it's compounded further, the mystery deepens because then Mr. Pantelic asked how many meetings of the Crisis Staff did you attend and so one is left with the impression that he was on the Crisis Staff so I've been waiting for clarification on those sorts of issues so I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you attend sessions of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BOZO NINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but what were you doing? That is the question the Prosecution is posing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, if you want to report for a news agency, you have to be able to obtain the information from those who have the information. If the journalist wishes to inform, then he goes to where the information can be found, together with the position. I couldn't go to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... What were you doing? Were you moving from institution to institution, collecting information? What were you doing? Just explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And so, what were you doing on a day to day basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that we started in late April to issue a paper, a bulletin, actually, which was printed in a rather primitive way because we did not have adequate equipment. It arrived only later on. And this was a full-time job. I was busy all day long. I had to write the bulletin, have it printed, and then further disseminate it in the surrounding villages and I went around by car. It took me a whole day to do that. I also had to contact with the journalists who came to the area, to try and provide them with the necessary information, and I also reported on the situation in the area pursuant to a request by the Tanug news agency. And I said I was also involved in the preparation of TV programmes, and in those days, it was only myself and Mr. Simeon Simic. We had to play all these roles. We were cameramen, we wrote the texts, were reporting from the field. We had to go to Belgrade, which was 200 kilometres away, and then go back to the office and do all the rest of the work. And it was a very demanding job, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry, I was waiting for the translation before asking my question. This bulletin that you mention that you started in late April, was this a bulletin which was, shall we say, was it an independent bulletin or newspaper, or was it a bulletin, newspaper, that was directed by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I guess you couldn't call it a Crisis Staff bulletin. It is true that it featured news in brief on what was going on at the time, but it doesn't mean that anyone from the Crisis Staff told us to write or not to write something. No. That never happened. The editor was Mr. Simeon Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm afraid we have to stop here so that we discuss some procedural matters and we shall continue tomorrow at 9.00. Tomorrow we are starting at 9.00. And I'd like the witness to be led out of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would like us to discuss a few things which concern the reorganisation of the Defence case. First of all, there are some motions by the Defence and I wanted to find out from the Prosecution -- I'm sure they've received them. The first one is regarding Mr. Miroslav Tadic's request for videolink for one of their witnesses, who they say is not in good health. I wanted to find out from the Prosecution whether there is any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I've only briefly discussed this with my colleagues. Might I just have another look at the motion just to refresh my memory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think that my answer will be no, we don't have a problem with it or objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is Mr. Grujicic Milutin, who was supposed to be the first witness viva voce for Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: He's the Croatian gentleman on the handling of exchanges, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that is the area of his evidence. Mr. Grujicic Milutin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and my learned colleague from the Prosecution, the gentleman is not from Croatia. We proposed the gentleman who is the president of the military commission of the 1st Krajina Corps, a Serbian witness who is supposed to testify live, viva voce. And depending on the videolink, I know this may not be important, but it is not necessary that he be the first one to testify. If the approval is given by the Trial Chamber, then I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We've got no problem with the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Trial Chamber will grant the motion for videolink, but as to the venue, that will be decided later because we want to see how many other witnesses may come under videolink and then it is easier for the Registrar and the administration to arrange one venue after that venue is cleared by all concerned parties, then the parties will be informed. I take it that that is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may help the Chamber, in light of his health condition, the witness lives in Sombor the town of Sombor which is located 100 kilometres from Belgrade, and any further movement, I think, could be more complicated in view of the condition of his health. I hope that the Chamber will bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because you did indicate in your motion that either Belgrade or Novi Sad would be appropriate. Very well. The Chamber will bear that in mind. The other motion is for more time for the demographic expert because of the problems mentioned in the motion getting the information required.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No objection, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. I have to say that on the relief requested on page 3, the English translation is not complete, in case the Defence does not -- I just wanted to clear that with the Defence right away. Or can I say this? That the Defence, if they have a hitch right at the beginning of next year, can they inform the Trial Chamber in writing so that we know -- we find -- we decide on the specific date when to expect this particular report? Although we haven't seen the other two expert reports do we take it that they will be filed by the 10th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for this omission in the text, in the last sentence of the text, but what I have to draw your attention to in respect of this analysis which is quite specific, because of the relationship and the fact that we need some documentation from the Prosecution, and not any other expert testimony, our problem with this particular expert testimony is as follows: As you have seen, we did receive the answer from OSC. However, we did not receive the response from the relevant authorities for statistics in BH. We wrote to them on several occasions but we haven't received any answer so far. So I'm afraid we are likely to have further problems. I will go to Belgrade soon and I will try to contact them directly over the telephone. We will inform the Chamber thereon because the information given by OSC doesn't really mean anything for us. In view of the fact that the documentation is with the OTP, I will ask the Trial Chamber to enable our expert to inspect, in a confidential manner, these documents in the Office of the Prosecutor because I'm afraid that if we asked the Chamber for the assistance, and if the Chamber then addresses itself to the relevant authorities there, that will take a lot of time. But if it is possible to have this comparison and analysis of the documents be done on the spot, in a confidential manner, that would significantly facilitate our problem. At any rate, I think we would be able to inform the Chamber immediately after Christmas whether we have received in the meantime any response from the relevant authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then, in that case, then, the Trial Chamber will make a ruling then and find out from the Prosecution whether what you have suggested can be done. Very well. Yes. The Trial Chamber has been observing the Defence so far, although it is only from Mr. Blagoje Simic, but there appears to be certain matters which are common to the Defence case, and I would like to find out from the parties and especially the Defence counsels themselves, since we are dealing with a matter which covers only one region. The evidence relating to ethnic tensions, which built up, up to the time of the armed conflict, the Trial Chamber is of the view that there isn't any difference in the way the case is being presented by the Prosecution as well as the Defence. There is no dispute from either party that there were ethnic tensions which built up leading to the time of the armed conflict. So that the Trial Chamber would like to -- the parties to avoid leading any evidence on this issue, unless there is something specific which attaches to the defence of a particular accused, otherwise generally I don't think that there is any contention in that -- on that point. On the arming, that different ethnic groups were arming themselves in the same period leading up to the armed conflict, again, the Trial Chamber is of the view that there doesn't seem to be any dispute in this regard, but I would like to ask the Prosecution to confirm, ethnic -- different ethnic groups were arming themselves in the period leading up to the armed conflict

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was a degree of that going on, amongst all three ethnic groups. The degree and the quality of that is another issue altogether and the extent of it on the part of one or more groups. That's another issue. That's another matter. But yes, there is generally no dispute that there was a lot of arms and weaponry in the municipality and a lot of people were -- of the three ethnic communities were purchasing and buying arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is no dispute with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No general dispute with that, no, and -- but I stress that the extent of it and the manner in which it was organised and done and the purpose and intent of it, well, that's another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can't speak of the intention or the purpose of it because there is no dispute that there was an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no. I appreciate that. Of course not, we don't dispute that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I know that the case of the Defence appears to be that those who were arrested or detained were found to have -- to be involved in an armed insurrection. That's a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because that is material as to when they were arrested and whether they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And just how many arms and just how serious the arming and -- sorry, potentially dangerous the arming of other groups was is also a matter that is to a certain extent contested between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But does it matter? Because this is a situation which led to the actual conflict itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, it doesn't matter particularly, but if you want the -- if the Prosecution's position is that the factual scenario is that the extent of arming amongst the Muslims, and in particular in the town of Bosanski Samac, was of a different quality, a different order, than the arming of the Serbian population, in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So how does that impact on the case of the Prosecution, if it is accepted that there was an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, it may not. I may not have a considerable impact on the presentation of the Prosecution case, but I just don't want to be seen to be making some sort of admission that there was -- the arming amongst the three ethnic groups of the same type, the same quality, the same extent, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. It's just the general situation which was occurring at that time, each ethnic group was arming themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are not discussing about the particular, the quality of arms or the particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How much arming was goes going on, how many guns and the quality, the superior weaponry, preponderance of weaponry, that sort of thing. There is no concessions made there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I just raise one other matter not related to that but the earlier issue that you raised, and that was ethnic tensions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You heard nothing from the Prosecution when you raised that and that is generally the position of the Prosecution, but I just remind you that at the beginning of the trial, there was some evidence from some of the witnesses regarding certain episodes that took place, particularly from Dragan Lukac who gave evidence and the import of his evidence and also from stuff, material from Todorovic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That indicated that some of the incidents -- the people who committed those episodes and people who were behind episodes leading to ethnic tension, and I think some of the other witnesses have also mentioned episodes. They point to certain episodes and say, "We think it was this group behind it or we think it was that group behind it." And I only raise that because the Defence may want to produce evidence about those specific episodes. For example, a kiosk was destroyed. You will recall that. There were power lines that were destroyed and Dragan Lukac gave evidence about some of the foot prints he found near the telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And that he thought it was the JNA, the explosive used and so on. It's those issues that the Defence should be free to attack, if they want to, by calling witnesses and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the specific incidents but not the general situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: However, the general situation, it is accepted, that there was a rise in ethnic tensions amongst all three groups. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just briefly say something in respect to what our colleague Mr. Di Fazio said, we were instructed as the Defence, all three Defences, by the Trial Chamber, not to challenge the part of the indictment that was not in force any more since it was dismissed through the motion for acquittal, in oral and also written decision with reasons, so we didn't have much witnesses and we didn't pay much attention to these events that related to the destruction of properties of non-Serb ethnicity. However, there were a couple of incidents involving shooting, involving wounding of some persons, that we would like to bring witnesses for. So we didn't deal with what the Trial Chamber ordered us not to take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That is on record, on the ruling under Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, Mr. Lazarevic, in terms of the destruction of power lines, it strikes me that that is a different matter to destruction of houses and businesses and so on, because in destroying the power lines, it would be like destroying a water system and what have you, in terms of its impact on the population as a whole in the town, in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand, Your Honours, that this is not something that the Prosecution gave hard evidence during their case that this incident could be related to any one of the defendants. Even their witnesses, they didn't actually say anything like that. They had some suspicions. Now, in particular, Dragan Lukac, who was chief of the police he actually admitted they didn't have any criminal record, they didn't put any criminal case in this respect, and so this is why we didn't have attention. And we also thought that this, if we go in these kind of details, it would take too much time of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's not the point. The point is simply meeting the Prosecution case, and what you have explained is actually -- is what is on record regarding the power lines. Yes. The other observation of the Trial Chamber is that the Defence of Mr. Blagoje Simic, who has got some witnesses under Rule 92 bis, if those -- those statements are not ready, the Trial Chamber may call upon the next defendant to start giving evidence, because we don't want to waste time. So what is important is to have the evidence on record. As to the sequence, it may not matter necessarily because the Rule 92 bis statements have to -- the Registry and the administration are also involved. So until those matters are resolved, it may be necessary to start with the evidence of one or the other accused persons, and I'm sure that the parties were informed about this. So what the Trial Chamber is asking is that the other two accused persons should be ready, if they are going to give evidence or if they have their viva voce witnesses. Of course, this will be indicated to avoid sending back witnesses without giving evidence. The other point is that in view of the matters that have been pointed out, where we don't need any evidence, the time to be taken by the rest of the witnesses, even with Mr. Blagoje Simic's evidence, may be cut down, because looking at the summaries, there is a -- there are common points for some witnesses. So that may be cut down so that we avoid wasting time unnecessarily. And the rest of the witnesses for the other two should also -- the counsel should also bear that in mind so that we don't repeat evidence which is not on matters which are not contested or where there is nothing in particular to the defence of a particular accused which is relevant to his defence, so that we can move on, and the Trial Chamber expects that once the decision on Rule 71 deposition witnesses is finally made, especially as to the venue, this also concerns the Registry, then we should be able to work out the schedule when we expect the Defence case to be completed or the trial to be completed. Unless there are some other matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if you allow me, please, I respectfully ask this Trial Chamber, and I would like to respectfully move this Trial Chamber with regard to some changes in my list of Rule 92 bis testimonies, due to some reasons because the people are not available, they are away, and we cannot locate them, like in pre-trial phase, I respectfully ask this Trial Chamber to grant the following motion: Speaking of the -- in my -- in my motion, joint Defence motion of November 26th, in Annex 1, under the number 3, there is a person, Jusufovic Jusuf, and now the Defence of Blagoje Simic would like to replace this person with another gentleman, Sego Drago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This person hasn't been on the list before at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact -- well, he was on the large list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- at the beginning, so everyone is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just being reorganised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And under number 6 in my Annex 1 of this joint motion is a witness Mrs. Nezirovic Dusanka, and we propose to replace her with another person, another lady, called -- just a moment -- Andric Pelka, Andric Pelka, because, Your Honour, we already informed the Registry with these changes in regard to 92 bis, so everything is fully in coordination with the Registry. Another thing, Your Honour, is character witnesses. Defence is not able to locate and to contact Dr. Mesud Nogic and, in fact, instead of Mr. Nogic, the Defence will call, under Rule 92 bis, Mr. Jusufovic Jusuf, who is already on the list 92 bis, but he can testify on the character of Mr. Blagoje Simic, so there are only these two small changes. Also I am informed by the Court officer that - and I do apologise on behalf of my team - that there are some typewriting problems and errors with regard to the name of Mr. Nijemcevic, Mitar. The right and exact family name and name is Nijemcevic, Mitar but not Nijemcevic, Dragan like it was mentioned in my earliest -- in my first motion. And we do believe that by this afternoon, we shall receive certificated translation from interpreters unit of the expert witness, handwriting expert, forensic witness, Dr. Aleksic. As a matter of courtesy, I already provided one copy of B/C/S language, I gave it to the Prosecution. It's not so big document, maybe six or seven pages, so I believe that by this afternoon we could have the translation, and hopefully it will be filed tomorrow. If not, Your Honour, maybe we could file B/C/S version, and then immediately while we are away, I can instruct the Registry and our colleagues to just attach translation, official translation, of that report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- to my motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As long as the report is filed, at least before we resume next year so that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No problem with that. In next couple of days maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To give the Prosecution sufficient time. Thank you. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To follow up on what my colleague Mr. Pantelic said, and it's a request of all of us, in connection with the psychological expert testimony, Dr. Leposava Kron has -- the report has been submitted and translated. In accordance with the Registry, we agreed -- the report itself consists of 30 or 40 pages. In order to facilitate the work of the translation unit here, the text of this report and the Barasin report and Professor Nikolic report, you said -- you saw that we had done the translation in Belgrade. So we agreed that we should provide the translation in order to facilitate the work here. So the report has been translated, but we should like to check the translation once again because it's a very technical text, and we should like the deadline to be extended until the 20th of December. We need only a couple of days when we get back to Belgrade to verify, to check, the translation, so we would like the deadline to be extended until the 20th of December, and by that time it will surely be filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection to the extension?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Then that is granted. Very well, we will continue our proceedings tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 4.28 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of December, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
